topicName: Feature Scaling: StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Feature Scaling: StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler in Scikit-learn"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Feature scaling is a crucial step in the data preprocessing pipeline of machine learning. Many machine learning algorithms perform poorly when numerical features are on drastically different scales. This tutorial explores three fundamental scalers provided by Scikit-learn: StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Why Feature Scaling Matters"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Algorithms that compute distances between data points, such as K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machines (SVMs), and K-Means clustering, are heavily influenced by the range of feature values. Gradient descent-based optimization algorithms (like Linear Regression and Neural Networks) also converge much faster when features are scaled."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"1. StandardScaler"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"StandardScaler assumes your data is normally distributed (Gaussian) and scales the features such that the mean becomes 0 and the standard deviation becomes 1. It is calculated using the formula: z = (x - u) / s, where u is the mean and s is the standard deviation."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

data = np.array([[1.0, 200.0], [2.0, 400.0], [3.0, 600.0], [4.0, 800.0]])
scaler = StandardScaler()
scaled_data = scaler.fit_transform(data)
print(scaled_data)"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. MinMaxScaler"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"MinMaxScaler bounds all the data within a specific range, typically between 0 and 1. This scaler is sensitive to outliers because extreme values compress the normal values into a very small range. It is defined as: x_scaled = (x - x_min) / (x_max - x_min)."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

scaler = MinMaxScaler(feature_range=(0, 1))
scaled_data = scaler.fit_transform(data)
print(scaled_data)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. RobustScaler"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"If your dataset contains many outliers, StandardScaler and MinMaxScaler may yield poor results due to skewed mean and variance calculations. RobustScaler removes the median and scales the data according to the Interquartile Range (IQR), making it robust to outliers."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler

data_with_outliers = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 3.0], [3.0, 2.5], [100.0, 50.0]])
scaler = RobustScaler()
scaled_data = scaler.fit_transform(data_with_outliers)
print(scaled_data)"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Using Scalers"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always split your data into training and testing sets before applying feature scaling."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use fit_transform() on the training data to learn parameters and transform it simultaneously."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use transform() only on the testing data to prevent data leakage from the test set into the training process."}]
